author: Grok Bot (for Mateo, pending review)
description: Sound money history, inflation, documented outcomes of central planning, why people immigrate to the US, evaluating promises, and money literacy for civic life. Non-partisan: no party/candidate endorsed or opposed; every lesson steelmans both sides. Learners, not students. Tax content is general only - consult a tax professional.

lessons.title: Sound Money Through History
lessons.topic: Money works best when people trust it to hold its value. Gold and silver were used for thousands of years because they are hard to make more of. When rulers secretly made coins with less silver, prices rose. Bitcoin's open rules cap its total supply at just under 21 million coins; new coins are still being created on a shrinking schedule until about 2140, and changing that rule would need almost the whole network to agree.
lessons.example: Roman emperors mixed cheaper metal into silver coins over about 250 years; people noticed and prices climbed.
lessons.activity: Look up pictures of a Roman denarius, a Weimar banknote and a Zimbabwe 100-trillion note. Make a timeline on paper and ask: what made people stop trusting each money?
check_questions: Why were gold and silver used as money?
What rule limits how many bitcoin can ever exist, and why is that rule hard to change?
lessons.steelman: FOR: Hard-to-change money protects savers and keeps rulers honest. AGAINST: Flexible money lets central banks respond to crises; fixed supply can be rigid and prices of Bitcoin swing a lot.
lessons.kid_explanation: Money works best when people trust it to hold its value. Gold and silver were used for thousands of years because they are hard to make more of. When rulers secretly made coins with less silver, prices rose. Bitcoin's open rules cap its total supply at just under 21 million coins; new coins are still being created on a shrinking schedule until about 2140, and changing that rule would need almost the whole network to agree.
lessons.parent_coach_insight: Documented: Roman denarius silver fell from roughly 90%+ under Augustus to only a few percent by the 270s AD. Weimar Germany 1923: about 4.2 trillion marks per US dollar by November. Zimbabwe 2008: a 100-trillion-dollar note was issued. Bitcoin's supply schedule is predictable, but that does not make its price stable: it is very volatile and can lose a lot of value. Not a price prediction or investment advice. Education, not financial advice. Learners practise only with practice coins or a pretend/test wallet (testnet or signet); no real bitcoin or sats for kids.
lessons.reflection_question: What makes me trust that money will still be worth something next year?
lessons.family_activity: Look up pictures of a Roman denarius, a Weimar banknote and a Zimbabwe 100-trillion note. Make a timeline on paper and ask: what made people stop trusting each money?
lessons.steelman_for: Hard-to-change money protects savers and keeps rulers honest.
lessons.steelman_against: Flexible money lets central banks respond to crises; fixed supply can be rigid and prices of Bitcoin swing a lot.
lessons.coherence_notes: Connects to Money & Mindset (assets, saving, cash flow), Thinking About Thinking (ask who pays, what would change my mind, steelman), Start Tiny (one small undoable step), and the Bitcoin anchor (fixed, verifiable rules vs. rules that can be changed quietly).

lessons.title: Inflation: Who Gets Hurt?
lessons.topic: Inflation means prices rise and each dollar buys less. People who save cash and those on fixed incomes get hurt most. People who own things that rise in price, or who borrowed money, may be hurt less.
lessons.example: Grandma remembers a candy bar for a few cents; look up today's price together.
lessons.activity: Ask a grandparent or elder what 3 items cost when they were young. Compare to today and calculate how many times more expensive.
check_questions: Who is hurt most by inflation?
lessons.steelman: FOR: Mild, predictable inflation is a stated goal of many central banks (about 2%) to encourage spending and avoid deflation. AGAINST: Even mild inflation quietly shrinks savings over decades, hurting those with least ability to invest.
lessons.kid_explanation: Inflation means prices rise and each dollar buys less. People who save cash and those on fixed incomes get hurt most. People who own things that rise in price, or who borrowed money, may be hurt less.
lessons.parent_coach_insight: Discuss the 'Cantillon effect': those who get new money first spend it before prices rise. US CPI data (BLS) is public; compare a gallon of milk today vs. 20 years ago. Avoid fear; build understanding and practical response (own assets, skills).
lessons.reflection_question: How would inflation change how I save?
lessons.family_activity: Ask a grandparent or elder what 3 items cost when they were young. Compare to today and calculate how many times more expensive.
lessons.steelman_for: Mild, predictable inflation is a stated goal of many central banks (about 2%) to encourage spending and avoid deflation.
lessons.steelman_against: Even mild inflation quietly shrinks savings over decades, hurting those with least ability to invest.

lessons.title: Central Planning in Practice
lessons.topic: In a centrally planned economy, the government decides what gets made, how much, and who gets it, instead of prices and voluntary trade. People have supported this for real reasons: they wanted fairness and an end to poverty. We can look at what actually happened and ask how the incentives worked. In the Soviet Union people often waited in long lines for goods. Cuba has used a ration book (the libreta) since 1962 for basic foods. Venezuela faced severe shortages and very high inflation, and millions of people left.
lessons.example: Cuba's libreta gives each household a small monthly ration of rice, beans, sugar and other basics at low prices; families often have to buy more elsewhere.
lessons.activity: Play a planning game: one parent 'planner' decides how many of each snack everyone gets for a week without asking. Then let each person trade freely. Talk about which felt fairer, which worked better, and what each way encouraged people to do.
check_questions: What is central planning, in your own words?
What is the libreta in Cuba, and what does it tell us about supply?
What are the strongest reasons people gave for supporting central planning?
lessons.steelman: FOR: People supported these systems hoping to end poverty, inequality and exploitation; supporters often point to gains in reading and basic healthcare. AGAINST: Documented results include chronic shortages, limits on personal and economic freedom, and mass emigration, partly because prices and incentives stop guiding what gets produced.
lessons.kid_explanation: In a centrally planned economy, the government decides what gets made, how much, and who gets it, instead of prices and voluntary trade. People have supported this for real reasons: they wanted fairness and an end to poverty. We can look at what actually happened and ask how the incentives worked. In the Soviet Union people often waited in long lines for goods. Cuba has used a ration book (the libreta) since 1962 for basic foods. Venezuela faced severe shortages and very high inflation, and millions of people left.
lessons.parent_coach_insight: This lesson is about how economic systems work: incentives and outcomes, not any current party, candidate or politician, and not a label for anyone's neighbors or relatives. Use the term 'central planning', not political labels. Steelman both sides honestly: supporters point to anger at inequality, real injustices before these systems, and reported gains in literacy and basic healthcare; critics point to shortages, lost personal freedoms and emigration. Note that every real economy mixes markets and government in different amounts. Stories about rations being skimmed come from people who lived in Cuba; share them as personal accounts, not verified fact. Venezuela: millions of people have left the country, and many families there have relatives abroad. Ask the learner how they would check whether any system delivers what it promises.
lessons.reflection_question: Why might people choose a system that promises fairness, and how would I check if it delivers?
lessons.family_activity: Play a planning game: one parent 'planner' decides how many of each snack everyone gets for a week without asking. Then let each person trade freely. Talk about which felt fairer, which worked better, and what each way encouraged people to do.
lessons.steelman_for: People supported these systems hoping to end poverty, inequality and exploitation; supporters often point to gains in reading and basic healthcare.
lessons.steelman_against: Documented results include chronic shortages, limits on personal and economic freedom, and mass emigration, partly because prices and incentives stop guiding what gets produced.

lessons.title: Why Millions Come to America
lessons.topic: Many millions of people living in the US were born in another country. Many come for opportunity, safety, rule of law and the chance to own property and start businesses. Some people also criticize the US as unfair. Both can be discussed honestly.
lessons.example: Interview a family member or neighbor who moved here (with their permission) about why they came and what surprised them.
lessons.activity: Make a two-column chart: reasons people come to the US, and fair criticisms people raise. Find one source for each item.
check_questions: Why do many people move to the US?
What is one fair criticism, and how could it be improved?
lessons.steelman: FOR: Rule of law, property rights and opportunity have drawn people for centuries; actions show what many value. AGAINST: Opportunity is not equal for everyone, and many countries have strengths the US lacks.
lessons.kid_explanation: Many millions of people living in the US were born in another country. Many come for opportunity, safety, rule of law and the chance to own property and start businesses. Some people also criticize the US as unfair. Both can be discussed honestly.
lessons.parent_coach_insight: Steelman both views: critics point to real inequality, past injustices and hard barriers; supporters point to property rights, courts, mobility and the revealed preference of immigrants. Avoid politics of immigration policy; focus on what draws people and how to weigh evidence.
lessons.reflection_question: What would make me want to move to a new country?
lessons.family_activity: Make a two-column chart: reasons people come to the US, and fair criticisms people raise. Find one source for each item.
lessons.steelman_for: Rule of law, property rights and opportunity have drawn people for centuries; actions show what many value.
lessons.steelman_against: Opportunity is not equal for everyone, and many countries have strengths the US lacks.

lessons.title: Evaluating Any 'Free' Promise
lessons.topic: Anyone can promise something free: companies, leaders, or people from any party. Smart thinkers ask three questions: Who pays? What does this encourage people to do? What will it cost in the long run?
lessons.example: A store says 'Buy one, get one free.' The family checks whether the first item's price went up.
lessons.activity: Collect 3 promises from ads, products or history (not from any current candidate or party campaign). Run each through: who pays, incentives, long-run cost. Rate how convincing each is.
check_questions: What are the three questions for any promise?
Why should we use them for every side?
lessons.steelman: FOR: Some promises do deliver real benefits that people judge worth the cost. AGAINST: Promises often hide costs or shift them to the future or to others.
lessons.kid_explanation: Anyone can promise something free: companies, leaders, or people from any party. Smart thinkers ask three questions: Who pays? What does this encourage people to do? What will it cost in the long run?
lessons.parent_coach_insight: Apply the same three questions to promises from every side; never single out a party. Practice with ads first, then any public promise. This builds civic judgment without telling anyone what to think. Keep examples to ads, products and historical cases; do not use current campaign promises.
lessons.reflection_question: Which promise did I believe too fast, and why?
lessons.family_activity: Collect 3 promises from ads, products or history (not from any current candidate or party campaign). Run each through: who pays, incentives, long-run cost. Rate how convincing each is.
lessons.steelman_for: Some promises do deliver real benefits that people judge worth the cost.
lessons.steelman_against: Promises often hide costs or shift them to the future or to others.

lessons.title: Checking Money Claims: A Family Fact-Check Habit
lessons.topic: Every day we hear claims about money: 'prices are up', 'this deal saves you money', 'everyone is buying this'. Understanding how money works lets you and your family check claims for yourselves before making money decisions, like what to buy, save or build. Tools: check the facts, ask who pays, and listen to the best version of the other side.
lessons.example: Made-up example: The family hears 'milk costs twice what it did five years ago.' They look up the price data together from an official source and decide whether the claim holds up before changing their grocery budget.
lessons.activity: Hold a family 'steelman night': pick a money question your family faces (save or spend, buy or rent, start a small project), each person argues the side they disagree with as well as they can, then check one fact together.
check_questions: How does understanding money help our family make better decisions?
lessons.steelman: FOR: People who understand money can better judge tradeoffs and claims made by anyone, including sellers, advertisers and people in power. AGAINST: Values, not just economics, shape decisions; experts disagree, and money knowledge alone does not settle every question.
lessons.kid_explanation: Every day we hear claims about money: 'prices are up', 'this deal saves you money', 'everyone is buying this'. Understanding how money works lets you and your family check claims for yourselves before making money decisions, like what to buy, save or build. Tools: check the facts, ask who pays, and listen to the best version of the other side.
lessons.parent_coach_insight: Strictly non-partisan: this lesson does not endorse or oppose any party, candidate or policy. Practice checking a claim with primary sources (BLS, Census, CBO). Focus on personal and family money decisions. Encourage respectful family discussions where each person steelmans the view they disagree with.
lessons.reflection_question: How do I know a money claim is true?
lessons.family_activity: Hold a family 'steelman night': pick a money question your family faces (save or spend, buy or rent, start a small project), each person argues the side they disagree with as well as they can, then check one fact together.
